questions.statement: Choose the correct option: 'I ___ reading a book right now.'
questions.context: English class in San Miguel, SV.

options.text: am
options.feedback: Correct! The subject of the sentence is 'I', and in the continuous form 'I' is always followed by 'am'.

options.text: is
options.feedback: 'is' goes with he, she, it and singular nouns, as in 'he is reading', so it does not fit 'I'.

options.text: are
options.feedback: 'are' goes with you, we, they and plural nouns, so 'I are reading' is not grammatical.

options.text: be
options.feedback: 'be' is the base form used after modals and in the infinitive; the continuous here needs the finite 'am'.

questions.explanation: Present continuous: I am + verb-ing.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: In 'The committee met to discuss the new budget,' why does the committee meet?
questions.context: English class in Soyapango, SV.

options.text: To discuss the new budget
options.feedback: Correct! The infinitive 'to discuss' names the purpose of the meeting, so it states directly why they gathered.

options.text: To decide who the members are
options.feedback: membership selection is never mentioned; the only stated purpose of the meeting concerns the budget.

options.text: To celebrate the end of the year
options.feedback: no celebration appears in the sentence, and the single purpose given is a working one.

options.text: To approve the meeting itself
options.feedback: the budget is what they met to discuss, not the act of meeting or its own approval.

questions.explanation: The infinitive after a verb of motion often expresses purpose. Reading 'to discuss the new budget' answers the why directly.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Identify the main idea: 'The text describes how bees help pollinate flowers and produce honey.'
questions.context: English class in Mejicanos, SV.

options.text: Bees are important for pollination and honey
options.feedback: Correct! The text names the two useful jobs of bees, pollinating flowers and producing honey, so that is its main idea.

options.text: Bees are dangerous insects
options.feedback: the text never says that bees are dangerous; it describes the useful work they do for flowers.

options.text: Honey is the only product bees make
options.feedback: the text also mentions pollination, so honey is not presented as the only product.

options.text: Flowers don't need bees
options.feedback: pollination depends on bees, so the text implies that flowers do need them.

questions.explanation: The main idea summarizes the key points about bees: pollination and honey.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which is the correct past form of 'go'?
questions.context: English class in Santa Ana, SV.

options.text: went
options.feedback: Correct! 'Went' is the irregular past simple form of the verb 'go'.

options.text: goed
options.feedback: 'goed' is not an English word; a past form is either regular or an irregular form already known.

options.text: gone
options.feedback: 'gone' is the past participle used after 'have' or 'has', not the past simple form.

options.text: going
options.feedback: 'going' is the -ing form used in the continuous, not a past form at all.

questions.explanation: 'Go' is an irregular verb: go → went (past simple).
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence uses the present simple correctly?
questions.context: English class in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: She goes to school every day.
options.feedback: Correct! In the present simple the third person singular of 'go' takes -es, so 'she goes' is the correct form.

options.text: She go to school every day.
options.feedback: after 'she' the verb needs the -s form, so this sentence is missing that ending.

options.text: She going to school every day.
options.feedback: 'going' belongs to the continuous form, but 'every day' requires the simple present.

options.text: She gone to school every day.
options.feedback: 'gone' is a past participle, and the sentence describes a habit, so the simple present is needed.

questions.explanation: Present simple: subject + verb(-s for he/she/it).
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Combine these sentences using a relative clause: 'A student designed the poster. Her drawing won the school competition.'
questions.context: English class in San Miguel, SV.

options.text: The student whose drawing won the school competition designed the poster.
options.feedback: 'Whose' expresses possession: the drawing belongs to the student.

options.text: The student who drawing won the school competition designed the poster.
options.feedback: 'Who' cannot express possession before 'drawing'; the clause needs 'whose drawing'.

options.text: The student which drawing won the school competition designed the poster.
options.feedback: 'Which' neither refers appropriately to this person nor expresses ownership of the drawing.

options.text: The student whom drawing won the school competition designed the poster.
options.feedback: 'Whom' marks an object referring to a person; it does not function as a possessive determiner.

questions.explanation: The relative clause identifies the student through her drawing. 'Whose' links the person to something she possesses.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: In 'She was meticulous about her notes,' what does 'meticulous' mean?
questions.context: English class in Santa Ana, SV.

options.text: Careful about details
options.feedback: Correct! 'Meticulous' describes someone who pays close attention to small details, which is exactly how she treats her notes.

options.text: Careless and hasty
options.feedback: this is the opposite of the word; being careless would mean skipping the details she actually checks.

options.text: Slow to speak
options.feedback: that describes how fast someone talks, and the sentence says nothing about the speed of her speech.

options.text: Eager to leave
options.feedback: it describes a wish to depart, while 'meticulous' here qualifies the care she takes with her notes.

questions.explanation: Context clues matter: 'about her notes' tells you the word describes the quality of her attention to detail, so 'careful about details' is the supported reading.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What is the main idea of 'Volunteers collected rubbish along the beach, and local schools planted twenty new trees'?
questions.context: English class in San Miguel, SV.

options.text: The community helped the environment
options.feedback: Correct! Both actions are environmental work carried out by local people, so the shared idea is community action for the environment.

options.text: The beach became crowded with visitors
options.feedback: the text never mentions visitors or crowding; it reports two organised clean-up and planting tasks.

options.text: The schools refused to plant trees
options.feedback: it states that schools planted twenty new trees, the opposite of what this option claims.

options.text: The volunteers complained about the rubbish
options.feedback: the sentence reports their collection of rubbish without describing any complaint from them.

questions.explanation: To find the main idea, group the details under one label. Rubbish collection and tree planting are both community work for the environment.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which is the correct past participle of 'write'?
questions.context: English class in Mejicanos, SV.

options.text: written
options.feedback: Correct! 'Written' is the irregular past participle, the form used after 'have' as in 'I have written it'.

options.text: writed
options.feedback: adding -ed to a short vowel plus a single consonant does not produce a valid participle; 'write' is irregular.

options.text: wrote
options.feedback: 'Wrote' is the past simple form, while the participle used with 'have' is 'written'.

options.text: writting
options.feedback: that double 't' spelling is a misspelling; the correct participle drops nothing and simply becomes 'written'.

questions.explanation: Regular verbs add -ed to the participle, but 'write' is irregular: write, wrote, written.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that uses the present continuous correctly.
questions.context: English class in Mejicanos, SV.

options.text: They are waiting for the bus now.
options.feedback: Correct! 'Right now' calls for the present continuous, and 'they' takes 'are' followed by the -ing form 'waiting'.

options.text: They wait for the bus now.
options.feedback: 'wait' is the simple present, which describes habits, but the time expression here points to this moment.

options.text: They are wait for the bus now.
options.feedback: after 'are' the verb needs its -ing form, and 'wait' on its own is the base form, not the participle.

options.text: They waited for the bus now.
options.feedback: 'waited' is the past simple, yet 'now' refers to the present moment rather than to a finished past action.

questions.explanation: Present continuous: am, is or are plus the -ing form, used for actions happening now or around now.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the correct option: 'My brother ___ his homework right now.'
questions.context: English class in Mejicanos, SV.

options.text: is doing
options.feedback: Correct! 'My brother' is third person singular, so the continuous needs 'is' plus the -ing form 'doing'.

options.text: are doing
options.feedback: 'are' goes with you, we and they, but a singular brother requires 'is' in this form.

options.text: does doing
options.feedback: 'does' never appears before an -ing form; that combination would belong to the simple present, as in 'he does his homework'.

options.text: did do
options.feedback: 'did' signals a finished past action, which contradicts the time expression 'right now'.

questions.explanation: Present continuous: am, is or are plus the -ing form. 'Right now' marks the action as unfinished at this moment.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Compare 'The volunteers who completed the training can enter' with 'The volunteers, who completed the training, can enter.' What difference do the commas make?
questions.context: English class in Santa Ana, SV.

options.text: Both sentences restrict entry to a subgroup, and the commas only indicate pauses.
options.feedback: The commas change the clause from identifying a subgroup to providing additional information about all the volunteers being discussed.

options.text: The first identifies eligible volunteers; the second says all the volunteers being discussed completed the training.
options.feedback: The defining clause selects trained volunteers, whereas the non-defining clause adds information about the whole referenced group.

options.text: The first describes future training; the second describes completed training.
options.feedback: Both clauses use 'completed', so both describe finished training; punctuation does not change their tense.

options.text: The first allows everyone to enter; the second excludes volunteers who trained.
options.feedback: The first restricts eligibility to trained volunteers, and the second does not exclude those volunteers.

questions.explanation: A defining relative clause identifies which members of a group are meant. A non-defining clause adds information about an already identified group.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence uses the present perfect correctly with 'already'?
questions.context: English class in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: She has already finished her project.
options.feedback: Correct! 'Has already' plus the past participle 'finished' forms the present perfect, which matches the time marker 'already'.

options.text: She already has finish her project.
options.feedback: after 'has' the verb must appear as the past participle 'finished', never as the base form 'finish'.

options.text: She already finished her project.
options.feedback: this is the present simple of 'finish' with an adverb placed before it, and it does not use the perfect at all.

options.text: She have already finished her project.
options.feedback: the subject 'she' requires 'has', so 'have' leaves the sentence ungrammatical in this form.

questions.explanation: Present perfect: have or has plus the past participle. Adverbs such as 'already', 'yet' and 'ever' usually sit between the auxiliary and the participle.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which rule correctly describes omitting a relative pronoun in a defining relative clause?
questions.context: English class in Mejicanos, SV.

options.text: It can always be omitted when its antecedent is a person.
options.feedback: A person's relative pronoun must remain when it is the subject, as in 'the student who arrived'.

options.text: It can be omitted when it is the object, as in 'the book I borrowed'.
options.feedback: 'I' is the subject of 'borrowed', and the omitted pronoun represents its object, 'the book'.

options.text: It can be omitted only when it expresses possession.
options.feedback: Possessive 'whose' must remain because it establishes ownership; omission applies to object relative pronouns.

options.text: It must be omitted whenever the clause uses the past tense.
options.feedback: Omission depends on the pronoun's grammatical role, not the tense of the relative clause.

questions.explanation: An object relative pronoun can be omitted in a defining clause. A subject relative pronoun cannot be omitted.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which question is formed correctly in the past simple?
questions.context: English class in San Miguel, SV.

options.text: Did you visit the museum last Saturday?
options.feedback: Correct! Past simple questions begin with 'did', followed by the base form 'visit' and the past time expression 'last Saturday'.

options.text: Did you visited the museum last Saturday?
options.feedback: after 'did' the verb returns to its base form, so the -ed ending in 'visited' is incorrect here.

options.text: Do you visit the museum last Saturday?
options.feedback: 'Do' builds present simple questions, and 'last Saturday' refers to a finished past time.

options.text: Were you visit the museum last Saturday?
options.feedback: 'Were' cannot stand in for 'did' before a lexical verb, because only 'be' takes that past auxiliary.

questions.explanation: Past simple questions use 'did' plus the base form. The -ed ending and the past time expression belong together, never after 'did'.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that combines 'We visited a library in Santa Ana' and 'Students can borrow laptops there' using a relative clause.
questions.context: English class in Mejicanos, SV.

options.text: We visited a library in Santa Ana which students can borrow laptops.
options.feedback: 'Which' alone cannot express the location here; the clause needs 'where' or 'in which'.

options.text: We visited a library in Santa Ana whose students can borrow laptops there.
options.feedback: 'Whose students' introduces possession and changes the relationship; the original describes borrowing at a location.

options.text: We visited a library in Santa Ana where students can borrow laptops.
options.feedback: 'Where' refers to the library as the place in which students can borrow laptops.

options.text: We visited a library in Santa Ana where students can borrow laptops there.
options.feedback: 'Where' already expresses the location, so adding 'there' duplicates that grammatical function.

questions.explanation: 'Where' introduces a relative clause describing what happens at a place. It replaces the location reference 'there'.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: In 'The soup smells delicious,' what does 'smells' express?
questions.context: English class in Mejicanos, SV.

options.text: Perception through the sense of smell
options.feedback: Correct! With 'smell' the linking verb relates the subject to a quality perceived by the nose, not an action performed on an object.

options.text: An action carried out on the soup
options.feedback: that would need a transitive verb with an object, but here the sentence describes how the soup is perceived.

options.text: A state that began in the past
options.feedback: nothing in the sentence points to a starting point in the past, so the past perfect reading does not apply.

options.text: A comparison between two soups
options.feedback: the sentence contains no second soup and no comparative structure such as 'than'.

questions.explanation: Some verbs such as 'look', 'feel', 'taste' and 'smell' work as linking verbs: they describe how the subject is perceived rather than an action.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What is the main idea of 'The bridge was closed for repairs, so the school bus took a longer route through the city'?
questions.context: English class in Santa Ana, SV.

options.text: A road closure changed the route of the school bus
options.feedback: Correct! The closure is presented as the cause and the longer city route as its direct effect on the bus.

options.text: The city has many bridges
options.feedback: the text names a single bridge and its closure; it makes no claim about how many the city has.

options.text: Repairs take longer than expected
options.feedback: nothing says the repairs were late, only that the closure forced a longer route.

options.text: The bus was late for school
options.feedback: the sentence explains the route change and never states that the bus arrived late.

questions.explanation: A cause-and-effect sentence names a problem and its result. Read the text as 'the closure caused the new route'.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: In formal English, which relative pronoun completes 'The researcher to ___ the students addressed their questions explained the results'?
questions.context: English class in Mejicanos, SV.

options.text: whose
options.feedback: 'Whose' expresses possession and cannot serve as the object of 'to' in this clause.

options.text: which
options.feedback: 'Which' normally refers to things, whereas the antecedent here is a person, 'the researcher'.

options.text: whom
options.feedback: 'Whom' is the object form used for a person immediately after the preposition 'to' in formal English.

options.text: that
options.feedback: 'That' cannot immediately follow a fronted preposition in a relative clause.

questions.explanation: Formal relative clauses use 'whom' for a person who is the object of a preceding preposition. The phrase 'to whom' identifies the recipient of the questions.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence correctly uses a non-defining relative clause to add information about Ana's brother?
questions.context: English class in San Miguel, SV.

options.text: Ana's brother, that lives in San Miguel, teaches mathematics.
options.feedback: 'That' is not used to introduce non-defining relative clauses enclosed by commas.

options.text: Ana's brother, who lives in San Miguel, teaches mathematics.
options.feedback: 'Who' refers to a person, and the paired commas mark the clause as additional information.

options.text: Ana's brother, lives in San Miguel, teaches mathematics.
options.feedback: The relative pronoun is the subject of 'lives' and cannot be omitted from this non-defining clause.

options.text: Ana's brother, which lives in San Miguel, teaches mathematics.
options.feedback: 'Which' refers to things rather than a person such as Ana's brother.

questions.explanation: A non-defining relative clause uses commas and an appropriate relative pronoun. 'Who' introduces additional information about a person.
questions.subject: ingles
